title: The eight limbs of yoga
hookLine: a baby falls into a praying woman's cupped hands, and grows up to set the breath fourth in line
carry: yoga begins with the yamas, not the breath

lines: EIGHT LIMBS. THE BREATH IS FOURTH.
cards: There's a well-loved legend about how Patanjali arrived. A devout woman named Gonika had cupped water in her palms to offer to the sun, praying for a child, and a tiny figure fell into her hands.

She called him Patanjali: pata, fallen, and anjali, cupped hands. Devotees say he was Adishesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. Some yoga schools still open class with a chant to him.
And his Yoga Sutra lays out yoga as eight limbs, in order. Anyone looking for breathwork might be surprised. The breath is fourth.

teach.h: HOW YOU TREAT PEOPLE COMES FIRST.
teach.b: First the yamas, restraints in how you treat others: non-harm, truth, not stealing, self-restraint, not grasping.
Then the niyamas, observances in how you treat yourself: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study, surrender to God. Then the seat. Then pranayama.

Then the senses drawn in, concentration, meditation, absorption. That order is one of the big teachings of Hindu yoga: it's a path to freedom, and it starts with how you treat people, before anyone counts a breath.

Look closer at the seat: posture should be steady and easy, a way of sitting that can be held without fuss. Once it's in place comes pranayama: a pause, a breaking, in the flow of in-breath and out-breath.

Through it, the sutras say, a covering over the inner light grows thin, and the mind becomes fit for concentration. Each step makes the next one possible. An honest, unharming life quiets the mind that sits down.

teach.h: A STEADY SEAT, THEN THE BREATH.
teach.b: A steady seat lets the breath settle. A settled breath lets the mind gather.

teach.h: EACH STEP MAKES THE NEXT POSSIBLE.
teach.b: Skip one and the next wobbles.

Many Hindu teachers say this is why yoga isn't only exercise: a breath class that skips non-harm and truth has skipped the first two limbs. The sutra doesn't list breathing exercises one by one; later manuals do.
What it gives is the frame, each limb laid on the last like stones in a path.

how: Where pranayama is taught in Patanjali's frame, it rests on the yamas and niyamas and follows posture work; some schools open with a chant to Patanjali, settle into a steady seat, move through gentle breath practices in order, and finish by resting in stillness or meditation.

o: the first and most important of yoga's eight limbs
breath practice built on a steady seat, step by step
a fast breathing drill done before any posture

games.q: a studio class jumps straight to breath holds and calls the rest of yoga 'optional extras'. what does patanjali's order say?
o: fine: the breath is the real yoga.
the path starts with the yamas and niyamas, then the seat, then the breath.
games.why: in the Yoga Sutra, pranayama is fourth; non-harm, truth and the rest come first, and each limb makes the next possible.

practice: Before you sit, choose one yama to carry today, non-harm or truth, and say it to yourself once.
Then shift until the sitting feels steady and easy; let each out-breath slow a little, noticing the small pause at the bottom of it, without holding.
If you pray, end with a bow to the teacher, as some schools do; if any step wobbles, go back one.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama sequences: breath practice in an order, the fourth of yoga's eight limbs, after the yamas, the niyamas and a steady seat.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: yama, restraint; the yamas, how you treat others, are the first of yoga's eight limbs.
